The file does not show any tests.
Empty inputs are handled in median, but the rest of the logic assumes at least one delivery model has data.

terms.meaning: The way a project is bought and run, such as a fixed-price contract, a design-and-build contract, or an owner-managed approach.
The project records this app links to, including contractors and the projects they worked on.
The middle value of a sorted list. It is less affected by one extreme value than an average.
A placeholder value used until real data exists. The screen labels it as such.

sections.name: File setup, Band, BAND_LABEL, Capability, CAPABILITY_LABEL, Priority, PRIORITY_LABEL
sections.title: Option types and labels
sections.what: Defines the choices a user makes in the advisor: project size band, owner team strength, priority, and novelty of the technology. It also gives each choice a plain-English label shown on screen.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the options and their wording in one place so the screen and the logic agree.
sections.watch_out: Each label table must cover every option, which the compiler checks for these tables. Adding an option means updating both its label table and the scoring tables.

sections.name: PROFILE
sections.title: Illustrative delivery model profiles
sections.what: Holds a hand-set score from 1 to 5 for each delivery model on certainty, speed, owner effort, flexibility, novelty handling, cost, and fit by project size. It also gives a short summary and three suggested setup steps for each model.
sections.why: Likely reason: no sourced measurements exist yet, so the file holds editable placeholder judgments. The file header says so.
sections.watch_out: These scores drive the ranking directly, so changing one number moves a recommendation without any supporting data behind it.

sections.name: PRIORITY_WEIGHTS, CAPABILITY_CAP
sections.title: Scoring weights and owner team limits
sections.what: Sets how much each priority (certainty, speed, cost, flexibility) counts toward a model's score. It also sets the most owner effort each team strength can handle: 2 for a lean team, 3.5 for moderate, and 5 for strong.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the scoring rules as visible data rather than buried in logic.
sections.watch_out: A lower owner effort limit penalises more models, so small edits here can reorder the whole list.

sections.name: median, Outcome
sections.title: Median helper and outcome type
sections.what: Finds the middle value of a list of numbers and returns nothing for an empty list. The outcome type describes a summary of overruns and delays: how many projects reported each, and their medians.
sections.why: Likely reason: medians are used so that one extreme project does not dominate the summary. The code does not state this.
sections.watch_out: The median returns nothing for an empty list, so callers must handle a missing value rather than assume a number.

sections.name: outcomes, Recommendation
sections.title: Building an outcome summary
sections.what: Takes a group of Yard projects and produces the summary: total count, how many reported a cost overrun or a delay, and the medians of those figures. Projects missing a figure are left out of that figure only.
sections.why: Gives the ranking evidence from real Yard records to compare delivery models.
sections.watch_out: The total count can be larger than the number of overrun or delay figures, because projects without those figures are still counted.

sections.name: recommend
sections.title: Ranking delivery models for a plan
sections.what: For one plan, scores every advisable delivery model. It reduces scores for models needing more owner effort than the team can give, adjusts for novelty and size, and boosts models Yard records show working in the same industry. It then converts the scores to fit numbers from 40 to 95 and sorts the best first, with plain reasons attached.
sections.why: Gives the owner an ordered answer with reasons rather than a single verdict.
sections.watch_out: Fit is relative: the best option on the list always reaches 95 and the worst always reaches 40, even when all options are weak. It is not an absolute quality rating.

sections.name: bandNote, hash, Backlog
sections.title: Size advice, fake-number helper, backlog type
sections.what: Returns one fixed piece of packaging advice based on project size. The hash helper turns any text into a repeatable number between 0 and 1. The backlog type describes a contractor's workload figures.
sections.why: Likely reason: the hash lets placeholder figures stay the same each time the same contractor is shown.
sections.watch_out: The size advice is illustrative guidance, not sourced. The hash always gives the same result for the same text, so placeholder figures will look consistent and may be mistaken for real ones.

sections.name: illustrativeBacklog, IN_DELIVERY, Experience
sections.title: Placeholder contractor workload figures
sections.what: Produces an invented backlog for a contractor: a value in billions, number of active projects, years of cover, and percent headroom. The figures come from the contractor's identifier and how many Yard links it has, not from any real records. The list of stage names counted as in delivery is also defined here.
sections.why: Likely reason: the advisor needs a workload column before real backlog data exists. The file header says the values are placeholders.
sections.watch_out: The numbers look like real figures, so anyone reading the advisor must notice the Illustrative label. Replacing this function with sourced data would change every ranking that uses headroom.

sections.name: experienceOf, Candidate
sections.title: Summarising a contractor's Yard record
sections.what: Gathers a contractor's linked Yard projects and counts them by industry, region, delivery model, and how many are currently in delivery. These counts feed the shortlist and the contractor details.
sections.why: Likely reason: comparing contractors needs a simple summary of each one's experience.
sections.watch_out: Links to projects that are not in the lookup are silently dropped, so a contractor can show less experience than its record lists.

sections.name: shortlist
sections.title: Choosing a shortlist of contractors
sections.what: Picks up to six contractors for the chosen delivery model. Firms with direct experience in the industry come first, ranked by a score mixing industry, region and model experience with placeholder headroom. Then come nearby firms that are active in the region but not the industry, only if they are catalogued.
sections.why: The comments say a square-root scale gives diminishing returns, so a very large home-market firm does not outrank firms already active in the chosen region.
sections.watch_out: The headroom part of the score uses invented figures, so the order within each group partly rests on placeholder values.

summary: Holds the logic behind the Build advisor: it ranks delivery models for a planned project and suggests a shortlist of contractors, mixing real Yard records with placeholder values that the screen labels Illustrative.
purpose: Helps an owner choose how to procure a planned build, by showing which delivery model fits their size, team, priorities and novelty, and which contractors have relevant experience.
why: Likely reason: the owner needs a ranked answer with reasons, not raw data. The file header says sourced Yard data and placeholder layers are kept apart on purpose.
how: 1. The file defines the option lists (project size, owner team strength, priority, novelty) and their labels. 2. It holds a fixed profile of 1 to 5 scores for each delivery model. 3. recommend scores each model using the owner's priority weights, penalises models that need more owner effort than the team can give, adjusts for novelty and size, and adds a boost for models Yard records show working in the same industry. 4. Scores are scaled to a 40 to 95 fit number and sorted. 5. shortlist ranks contractors by industry, region and model experience, with a placeholder headroom factor. 6. Helper functions compute medians and outcome counts.
inputs: A plan (industry, region, size band, owner team strength, priority, novelty), the Yard data (projects and contractor firms), and for shortlist the delivery model chosen.
outputs: A sorted list of delivery models, each with a fit score, plain reasons, and Yard outcome statistics; and a list of up to six contractor candidates with scores and placeholder backlog figures.
risks: The profile scores, backlog figures and packaging advice are invented placeholders. A fit score of 95 means best of the options tested, not a good result. Shortlist order partly depends on invented headroom values.
debug: If a ranking looks odd, first check the PROFILE table and PRIORITY_WEIGHTS for the model in question. If a contractor is missing, check that the firm has links to projects that exist in the lookup. If the medians look wrong, check that overrun and delay values are numbers and not missing.
